speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To begin assessing this newborn's generalized rash, when did you first notice the appearance of these spots?

speaker: Patient
text: 4-day-old newborn. The newborn was born at term with no complications. The mother had no prenatal care and has a history of gonorrhea treated 4 years ago. The newborn presents with a generalized rash that has been present for 1 day.

speaker: Doctor
text: Are the lesions purulent, vesicular, or pustular, and have you noticed any eye discharge or nasal congestion? REQUEST TEST: Gram stain of lesion exudate.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Gram stain of lesion exudate: Positive for Gram-negative diplococci consistent with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Generalized erythematous maculopapular rash and pustules. I also have Rash with an erythematous base, Rash over the trunk and extremities, Sparing of the palms and soles. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Pneumonia and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Congenital Syphilis

The clinical presentation of a generalized maculopapular rash with pustules on an erythematous base, combined with the maternal history of treated gonorrhea (a marker for potential STI exposure) and the specific finding of rash sparing the palms and soles, is classic for congenital syphilis. The previous suggestion of pneumonia was likely a misinterpretation of the systemic infection or a concurrent issue, but the skin findings are the primary diagnostic clue here. Given the mother's lack of prenatal care, we must immediately investigate for syphilis to prevent severe complications like snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, or bone abnormalities.

REQUEST TEST: Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) titer and VDRL.
REQUEST TEST: Darkfield microscopy of lesion exudate.
REQUEST IMAGES: Full body skin exam photograph.
